analysis.one_liner: Cuts off federal student aid to for-profit colleges and tightens nonprofit-conversion rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make for-profit colleges ineligible for federal student aid, ending the main revenue stream for schools like those whose students historically have high loan default rates. It would also disqualify any school whose owners filed for bankruptcy, whose executives were convicted of aid fraud, or whose officers previously ran a school that shut down. And it would set new standards for schools trying to convert from for-profit to nonprofit status, requiring public notice and review, after several high-profile conversions in which former for-profit owners kept financial ties.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and prospective students, especially those at for-profit colleges, who would no longer be able to use federal loans and grants at schools with poor outcomes; and taxpayers, who would no longer back loans at schools with high default and fraud rates.

how_it_helps.text: Makes all for-profit institutions of higher education ineligible to receive federal student assistance.

Disqualifies any school that has filed for bankruptcy, been convicted of a crime involving federal student aid, committed fraud or substantial misrepresentation, or whose executive officers previously worked at a school that closed while receiving federal aid.

Caps enrollment limits that target common for-profit practices: no more than 50% of students in distance-education courses, no more than 25% incarcerated students, and no more than 50% students without a high school diploma, plus a requirement that certificate programs prepare students for gainful employment.

Sets standards for converting a for-profit school to nonprofit status, requiring that former owners were not overpaid for assets, that no one with power over the governing board profits from the school, and that the application be published in the Federal Register for public comment before approval.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies and their investors, which rely on federal loans and grants for most of their revenue, would lose that income; students enrolled at those schools would have to find other programs or pay out of pocket, though the bill lets foreign-school students finish out one academic year after a school loses eligibility.

drawbacks.text: The ban is a blunt instrument: it cuts off aid at every for-profit school, including legitimate career and technical programs, and students at disqualified schools would lose access at institutions they may already be attending.

The 50% cap on distance-education enrollment applies to all schools, not just for-profits, which would force large changes at public and nonprofit online universities that enroll mostly remote students.

Disqualifying a school because an executive once worked at a school that closed, or because the school or an affiliate filed for bankruptcy, could sweep in institutions by history or technicality rather than current misconduct.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students, the benefit is real: for-profit colleges have long accounted for a disproportionate share of federal loan defaults and fraud cases, and cutting off aid attacks the revenue stream directly. The cost is also real: the bill offers no transition path for enrolled students at domestic schools, and some of its disqualification triggers and enrollment caps are broad enough to hit schools and students beyond the worst actors. A narrower version targeting documented fraud and conversion self-dealing would carry less collateral damage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on October 17, 2019, with seven original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
Sixteen Democrats total cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The committee held no hearing, took no markup, and reported no vote; no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit college companies keep full access to federal student aid, and taxpayers continue backing loans at those schools, including schools later found to have defrauded students. Students at for-profit colleges gained nothing from the bill's death; the aid rules it would have changed remain as they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit college companies, which keep federal aid

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip federal student aid from for-profit colleges and set nonprofit-conversion standards.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it stayed in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.what_they_did: The sector's trade association and member companies actively lobby against restrictions on their access to federal student aid, as they did during the Obama-era gainful employment fight.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 supporters (the sponsor and 16 cosponsors) were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic-run committee declined to move the bill.

industries.note: These schools collect most of their revenue from federal loans and grants; the bill would cut that off entirely. Students at these schools often take on debt for credentials with weak labor-market payoff, so the industry's interest in keeping aid flowing runs directly against the students' interest in affordable, quality programs.

industries.industry: Companies converting for-profit schools to nonprofits
industries.note: The bill would require independent valuations, ban financial benefits to people who control the board, and force public comment on every conversion. It targets the practice of former for-profit owners retaining profitable service contracts after their school 'becomes' a nonprofit.
The 50% cap on distance-education enrollment would apply to these schools too, forcing curriculum changes at institutions that serve remote students legitimately.
